properties.name: Egypt grain belt
properties.one_line: Egypt's Nile floodplain fed Rome for roughly four months of every year, shipped north through Alexandria's twin harbors. Grain freighters like the Isis could carry over 1,200 tons in a single hold, a capacity no ship matched again until the 1800s. Augustus made Egypt his personal province precisely to guard this lifeline, and a bad Nile flood meant hunger in the streets of Rome.

properties.name: Africa Proconsularis grain belt
properties.provinces: Africa Proconsularis (coastal and interior Tunisia, NE Algeria)
properties.one_line: Africa Proconsularis grew enough rain-fed wheat to feed Rome for eight months of the year, complementing Egypt's four. Strabo, Pliny, and Josephus all praised the quality of its grain, grown on latifundia across the fertile Byzacena and Zeugitana districts. Convoys of grain ships left Carthage's hinterland ports for the Tiber every sailing season.

properties.name: Sicily grain belt
properties.one_line: Sicily was Rome's original grain island, feeding the city for two centuries before Egypt entered the picture. Prosecuting the corrupt governor Verres in 70 BCE, Cicero called the island 'a nurturer of our populace, a granary for our provinces.' Verres extorted so much grain from Sicilian farmers that output collapsed, a scandal serious enough to end his career.

properties.name: Baetica grain belt
properties.one_line: The Guadalquivir valley grew so much wheat and barley that Baetica ranked among the empire's breadbaskets by the 2nd century, alongside its famous oil and wine. Grain barges moved downriver to the Atlantic port of Hispalis (Seville) for onward shipment. Roman surveyors laid its fields out in a centuriated grid whose lines still show up in aerial photographs of Andalusia today.

properties.name: Pannonia grain belt
properties.one_line: The Danube plains of Pannonia carried wheat, spelt, and barley from imperial estates to the legion camps strung along the frontier. Barges floated grain downriver to feed forts from Vindobona to Aquincum, tying the frontier's food supply to its own farmland. Excavated ovens at Roman Mursa (Osijek) held some 24,000 charred cereal grains, a direct snapshot of one harvest.

properties.name: Baetica olive belt
properties.one_line: Baetica supplied more olive oil to Rome than any other province, shipped north in globular Dressel 20 jars stamped with the producer's name. Broken amphorae from this one trade route built Monte Testaccio, an artificial hill in Rome over 35 meters tall made of an estimated 53 million discarded oil jars. More than 80 percent of that hill came from Baetica alone.

properties.name: Tripolitania olive belt
properties.one_line: The dry Tarhuna plateau behind Leptis Magna was covered in olive groves worked by tenant farmers on estates owned by the city's elite. Archaeologist Richard Goodchild counted over 200 individual olive-press ruins scattered across that one hinterland district alone. Julius Caesar once fined Leptis three million pounds of oil as a war indemnity, implying roughly a million bearing trees already stood in the ground.

properties.name: Istria olive belt
properties.one_line: Istria's red soil produced an olive oil the Romans ranked among the finest in the empire, exported in amphorae made from local clay at kilns like Fazana. Villas rustica lined the peninsula's coast to process and ship the harvest straight from the groves. Sunken amphorae still turn up on the Adriatic seabed off Pula, wrecks from the oil convoys that once left its harbor.

properties.name: Attica olive belt
properties.one_line: Attica's olive groves were Athens's oldest export industry, protected since Solon banned exporting any other farm produce to preserve them for oil. The sacred olive on the Acropolis, said to be Athena's own gift to the city, stood before the Erechtheion as a living civic symbol. Victors at the Panathenaic Games still went home with amphorae brimming with Attic oil as their prize.

properties.name: Syria olive belt
properties.provinces: Syria (coastal hinterland and northern limestone hills)
properties.one_line: Syria's coastal hills and the limestone uplands inland from Antioch carried olive groves worked with rock-cut presses suited to the rugged terrain. Farmers at sites like Majduliyya in the Golan cut crushing basins straight into bedrock rather than build separate press houses. Production served the province's own large population first, with Antioch itself among its biggest markets.

properties.name: Falernian wine belt
properties.one_line: The slopes of Mount Falernus produced the wine Roman poets ranked above every other vintage in Italy. Pliny the Elder distinguished three separate crus by altitude on the same hillside, and Horace, Martial, and Catullus all wrote it into verse. The best vintages reportedly aged for a century and were said to be strong enough to catch fire near an open flame.

properties.name: Chian and Lesbian wine islands
properties.one_line: Chios and Lesbos exported the most sought-after wines of the Greek Aegean, shipped west in amphorae stamped with each island's own seal. Chios marked its jars with a sphinx to stop mainland forgeries, and its wine was poured at four separate Roman triumphs, the first foreign vintage ever served at one. Lesbian wine had rivaled Chian since Homer's day and stayed prized through the 2nd century.

properties.name: Rhaetic wine belt
properties.one_line: The vineyards around Verona, in the Alpine foothills bordering Rhaetia, produced a wine Virgil ranked second only to Falernian in the Georgics, telling growers not to 'rival Falernian cellars' with it, high praise by that comparison alone. The grape could not be cultivated successfully outside this one hill district. Modern Refosco is thought to descend from the same vine.

properties.name: Vienne wine district
properties.one_line: Vienne, once capital of the Gallic Allobroges before becoming a Roman colony, grew a black grape Pliny the Elder called the allobrogica, prized for its heavy yield and cold tolerance. Martial nicknamed the town 'wine-flavored' in his epigrams. Vineyards along the Rhone at Vienne and neighboring Seyssuel mark one of the earliest expansions of viticulture into Roman Gaul.

properties.name: Baetica wine belt
properties.one_line: Baetica exported wine alongside its famous olive oil, packed into distinctive ovoid amphorae and floated down the Guadalquivir and Genil to Atlantic ports. Residue analysis of Late Republican Baetican jars has confirmed grape derivatives sealed with pine-resin pitch, the standard Roman method for waterproofing a cask. By the 2nd century Baetica shipped wine as far as Britain and the Rhine frontier alongside its oil.

properties.name: Hercynian Forest timberland
properties.provinces: Free Germania beyond the Rhine/Danube frontier
properties.one_line: Tacitus described the Hercynian Forest as a vast wooded belt running nine days' march wide and sixty long along Rome's Germanic frontier. Garrisons on the Rhine and Danube limes cut its oak and fir for fort palisades, bridge piles, and firewood. The forest marked the edge of directly governed territory, real timber wealth just beyond ground Rome never fully annexed.

properties.name: Lebanon cedar forest
properties.one_line: The cedars of Mount Lebanon had supplied Mediterranean shipbuilders and temple-builders for two thousand years before Rome arrived, prized for wood that resists both rot and insects. Roman engineers cut the forest for ship timber and monumental roof beams across Syria and beyond. So much first-growth cedar was felled over the centuries that only isolated stands survive on the mountain today.

properties.name: Corsica pine forest
properties.one_line: Corsica's interior mountains grew tall stands of pine and fir that Roman shipwrights prized for masts and hull timber. The naturalist Theophrastus recorded Romans hauling Corsican logs to Italy lashed into one giant raft rigged with as many as fifty masts and sails. The island's straight, resin-rich trunks kept supplying western Mediterranean fleets for centuries.

properties.name: Apulian sheep transhumance corridor
properties.one_line: Every autumn hundreds of thousands of sheep flooded down the tratturi from the Samnite highlands to winter on Apulia's Tavoliere plain, and the region's wool trade was built entirely on that seasonal migration. Pliny and Columella both singled out the local breed for the fineness of its fleece. Varro wrote proudly of his own flock of 700 making the same trip every year. The drove roads mattered enough to the economy that towns aligned their streets around them.

properties.name: Numidian horse country
properties.one_line: The plains south of Carthage bred small, wiry horses ridden bridleless with nothing but a rope around the neck, prized for speed over open ground. Livy called their riders simply the best horsemen in Africa. Hannibal's cavalry made them feared enemies of Rome; by 117 CE entire Roman auxiliary cavalry wings recruit both mounts and riders straight from these same herds.

properties.name: Cisalpine cattle country
properties.provinces: Regio XI Transpadana / Regio VIII Aemilia (Po valley)
properties.one_line: The drained floodplain of the Po produced some of Italy's richest pasture, and by Strabo's account this was one of the most prosperous regions in the whole empire. Grain, wine and cattle all thrived on marshland Roman engineers had been reclaiming since the conquest two centuries earlier. Cisalpine hides and beef helped supply the legions stationed on the nearby Danube frontier.

properties.name: British hunting dog country
properties.one_line: Roman writers prized one British export above almost everything else the island produced: its hunting dogs. Strabo listed them among Britannia's valuable goods even before the conquest. The poet Oppian later described the fierce, tattooed-tribe-bred Agassian breed as unmatched at tracking game, and Tacitus counted clever hunting dogs alongside grain, hides and slaves as one of the province's chief exports.

properties.name: Jericho and Ein Gedi oases
properties.one_line: The oases around Jericho and Ein Gedi grew the ancient world's most prized dates, so rich that Pliny ranked the region's soil second only to Jerusalem's own. The same narrow strip produced balsam, distilled into the most expensive perfume in antiquity, and pomegranates famous enough to make the Bible's list of the land's seven blessed crops. Roman troops burned much of the Ein Gedi balsam groves during the Jewish War, but by 117 CE the plantations are back in full production.

properties.name: Fayum date groves
properties.one_line: Egypt's Fayum oasis, watered by a channel diverted from the Nile since Pharaonic times, filled with dense palm groves alongside the grain that made the province famous. Surviving papyri from private estates like the steward Zeno's record harvest yields and land leases in exacting bureaucratic detail, and poll-tax receipts from the reigns of Augustus and Tiberius survive from the same district. Dried Fayum dates traveled well enough to reach markets across the eastern Mediterranean.

properties.name: Cyrenaican silphium coast
properties.one_line: For centuries Cyrenaica's silphium plant was the single most valuable crop in the Mediterranean, a wild herb prized as medicine and seasoning that Cyrene stamped on its own coins. It grew in only one narrow coastal strip and resisted every attempt at cultivation elsewhere. Pliny records that the very last stalk ever found was sent to the emperor Nero as a curiosity — by 117 CE the plant that built Cyrene's fortune is already a memory, not a crop.

properties.name: Carian fig country
properties.one_line: The dried fig took its Latin name, caricae, directly from this stretch of Asia Minor's coast — proof of how completely Rome associated the fruit with Caria. The port of Kaunos shipped them out by the boatload alongside salted fish and resin, a trade already old by the time of the Delian League five centuries earlier. A Carian fig could travel to a Roman table months after harvest and still taste of home.

properties.name: Alpine fir forests
properties.one_line: The high slopes of the Alps grew silver fir prized above almost any other wood for ships' masts, light and strong enough that Pliny the Elder singled it out by name as ideal for shipbuilding. Roman engineers pushed roads deep into valleys that had never carried wheeled transport just to haul the timber out. A single mast could travel hundreds of miles from an Alpine hillside to a naval shipyard on the Mediterranean coast.

properties.name: Bruttium fir forest
properties.one_line: The mountains of Bruttium at Italy's southern tip carried one of the peninsula's last great stands of old-growth fir and pine, close enough to the coast to feed shipyards directly. Dendrochronological studies of shipwreck and building timber have traced planking back to these very slopes. By 117 CE the forest had already been logged hard enough that Rome treated what remained of the silva Sila as a resource worth guarding.
